newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl presents unity memoir on 14th year in power.
newsitem.headline: Kohl presents unity memoir on 14th year in power.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, celebrating 14 years in power on Tuesday, presented a 488-page memoir of his greatest triumph, Germany's peaceful reunification in 1990.
The book, written with two journalists from the popular newspaper Bild, was released just weeks before Kohl reaches another milestone and becomes the longest-serving post-World War Two chancellor.

"Ich wollte Deutschlands Einheit" (I Wanted Germany's Unity) divulged no secrets about the hectic months between mid-1989 -- when East Germans began deserting the country -- and the final merger of the divided states on October 3, 1990.

But it was the first time that Kohl, who in private often regales politicians and journalists with his memories of those dramatic days, has come out with an authorised version of the events that made him the leading statesman in Europe.
"Chancellor Kohl's version comes late, but thankfully not too late," Professor Hans Meier said at the presentation in Bonn. "It makes clear what a tightrope walk unification was."
Kohl, 66, became Bonn's chancellor on October 1, 1982, at a time when Europe's Cold War division seemed to be deepening as NATO and the Warsaw Pact installed new nuclear missiles.

On October 30, he will surpass the long service record of his political mentor, Konrad Adenauer, who founded Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party and served as West Germany's first chancellor from 1949 to 1963.
What stands out in Kohl's book are the personal insights he gives into the other leaders involved in the multilateral efforts to fit German unity into an international context.
The British prime minister of the day, Margaret Thatcher, who was his most vocal Western critic, "lived in the time before Churchill, in the balance of power thinking of the 19th century", he said.
"She just could not accept that Germany could end up as the big winner at the end of a century in which it had been defeated in two world wars," he added.

The late French president, Francois Mitterrand, who first hesitated and then discussed with Thatcher and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev ways of slowing down the Germans, emerges finally as a loyal friend and ally of Kohl's.

But, while the chancellor could pardon his caution, he made clear he did not appreciate the leading role Mitterrand took in pressuring him to recognise even before unification the Oder-Neisse line marking the post-war border with Poland.
Kohl insisted only an all-German parliament could renounce the eastern lands taken away from Germany after World War Two.
"I think Francois Mitterrand simply got it wrong in judging the concrete situation," he said.

Other leaders of the time, George Bush of the United States, Jacques Delors at the European Union's executive commission, and Felipe Gonzalez and Charles Haughey, the prime ministers of Spain and Ireland respectively, came in for praise for their strong support for Kohl's plan to reunite his homeland.
Bush's secretary of state, James Baker, who played a key role in the "Two-Plus-Four" talks restoring German sovereignty, "had what it takes to become president himself", Kohl commented.

In one of the many passages about his talks with the then Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev, Kohl reveals the Soviet KGB and East Germany's Stasi tried to provoke Moscow into a crackdown one day after the Berlin Wall fell.

Kohl tells how Gorbachev telephoned him for reassurance during a hastily organised rally in West Berlin on November 10, 1989, to check reports he was getting that outraged masses were storming Soviet army bases in East Germany.

He reassured the Soviet leader the mood was "like at a family party" and added: "Only later did I learn that Gorbachev had been deliberately fed false information. Opponents of reform in the KGB and Stasi wanted to provoke a military intervention by the Soviet troops stationed in East Germany."
"To this day I am very grateful to Gorbachev for not listening to the agitators," Kohl wrote.
